answer.label: Not A. A. Milne — actually Benjamin Hoff
answer.authorDates: b. 1946 · American author of “The Tao of Pooh”
answer.sourceLine: Benjamin Hoff wrote this exchange for his 1982 bestseller “The Tao of Pooh,” putting the words in the mouths of Milne’s characters to make a Taoist point. Quote Investigator ↗ found the lines in none of A. A. Milne’s four Pooh books — the Milne credit is a later mistake.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: “Lots of people talk to animals,” said Pooh. “Maybe, but . . .” “Not very many listen, though,” he said. “That’s the problem,” he added.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the dialogue to Benjamin Hoff’s “The Tao of Pooh” (1982) and states it appears in none of Milne’s canonical Pooh books.
QI notes the misattribution hardened by 2000, when “The New Encyclopedia of Christian Quotations” printed a condensed version crediting Milne.
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads ↗ still list the line under A. A. Milne, spreading the error.
source.excerptNote: The exchange is between Hoff’s narrator and Pooh in “The Tao of Pooh” — Hoff’s own invention, not a line lifted from Milne.

author.name: Benjamin Hoff
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 1946 · American author of The Tao of Pooh (1982)
author.bio: Benjamin Hoff is an American writer best known for The Tao of Pooh (1982) and its sequel The Te of Piglet (1992), which use A. A. Milne’s characters to explain Taoist ideas. He wrote this exchange himself, ventriloquizing Pooh — which is why readers later mistook it for Milne’s own words.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The line is endlessly pinned on A. A. Milne, the creator of Winnie-the-Pooh — but the words were written more than half a century after Milne’s Pooh books, by a different author entirely.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports the dialogue appears in none of Milne’s four Pooh books (“When We Were Very Young,” “Winnie-the-Pooh,” “Now We Are Six,” “The House at Pooh Corner”) and was written by Benjamin Hoff in 1982.

items.scope: Condensed “Some people talk to animals. Not many listen” variant
items.why: A shortened form crediting Milne circulated after “The New Encyclopedia of Christian Quotations” (2000) printed it, per Quote Investigator ↗; it too traces back to Hoff’s text, not Milne.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Benjamin Hoff’s, from “The Tao of Pooh” (1982) — a Pooh-flavored line that isn’t actually Milne’s, as Quote Investigator ↗ documents.

context.heading: Why it gets mistaken for Milne
lead: Hoff built The Tao of Pooh around dialogues between his narrator and Milne’s characters, writing new lines in Pooh’s voice to illustrate Taoist principles. This ventriloquism was so convincing that quotations from Hoff’s book — including this one — routinely get re-credited to the original creator of Pooh.
The result is a classic “magnet name” effect: a warm, quotable line about listening drifts to the more famous author, and quote sites copy the error from one another until the true source disappears.
context.pull: A line written in Pooh’s voice — but not by the man who created Pooh.
